title: Rendering Modes in Next.js
summary: Map CSR, SSR, SSG, ISR, and partial prerendering to Next.js routes, read the build's route table, and choose a mode for each page.
intro: The React course compared four ways to make a page's HTML: in the browser (CSR), on every request (SSR), at build time (SSG), and at build time with regeneration (ISR). Next.js does all four, plus partial prerendering, which mixes them inside one page. You don't pick a mode with a setting. You pick it by how you write each part of a page, and the build tells you what you got. This lesson reads the build's route table, then goes through static pages, dynamic pages, partial prerendering, and client rendering and static export, so you can choose a mode for each of Trailhead's pages and check it.

steps.title: Reading the route table
steps.body:
Every `next build` ends with the route table, and it's the one place that tells you, for every page at once, how it will be served. Learn to read it, and you'll catch a page that became slow, or a cache that stopped working, before your users do.

## The three symbols

- `○` **Static**: the whole page was rendered during the build, and every visitor gets that same HTML until it's revalidated. This is SSG, or ISR when a lifetime is shown.
- `◐` **Partial Prerender**: the page has a static shell, rendered during the build, with holes that are filled in on each request and streamed. This is partial prerendering, PPR.
- `ƒ` **Dynamic**: nothing of the page is kept ahead of time. It's rendered on every request, which is SSR. Route Handlers that answer POST, and pages that set `export const instant = false`, show up here.

The legend under the table prints only the symbols that appear in it. When a dynamic segment's values were listed ahead of time, the table shows the route, its shared App Shell, and the listed pages under it, counting the rest as `[+10 more paths]`.

## What decides each one

Next.js doesn't ask you to declare a mode. It renders every route during the build and records what happened:

- Everything finished during the build: `○`.
- Something waited for the request, inside a `Suspense` boundary: a hole, so `◐`. That something is request data like `cookies()` or `searchParams`, uncached data, or `connection()`.
- The route opted out with `instant = false`, or it's a handler for a method like POST: `ƒ`.

So a single component can change a whole page's symbol. The example below is Trailhead's table after the header got a cart count that reads the visitor's cookie. The header is in the root layout, so every page now has that hole, and every page that was `○` is `◐`. The rest of each page is still prerendered, and the shell still arrives at once. The table is telling you the truth: no page is the same for every visitor anymore.

## The Revalidate and Expire columns

For pages with cached data, the table shows the shortest `revalidate` and `expire` of everything in the page's shell, from the caching lesson. A blank means the shell never goes stale on a timer, only when a tag or path is revalidated.

## First-load JavaScript

Older versions of Next.js also printed how much JavaScript each page downloads on its first visit. Next.js 16 dropped that column, so measure it in other ways: the Network panel, filtered to JS, on a production build, or `next analyze`, which opens an interactive map of what's in each bundle and why. JavaScript matters most on pages people land on from a search or a shared link, since they pay for all of it before the page responds, so check those pages when you add a client component or a library.

examples.title: Every page with a hole
examples.prompt: Trailhead's route table after the header started showing a cart count read from the visitor's session. The `sed` at the end prints from the route table on.
examples.explanation: Every page is `◐` now, `/about` and `/catalog` included, which were `○` before. Nothing about them changed except the header they share. `/` still shows `1h` and `1d`, because its product list is cached, and the product pages show `1m` and `1h` from their reviews. `ƒ /api/revalidate` is the webhook from the caching lesson. The `○` symbol has dropped out of the legend, since no page uses it. Whether that's a problem depends on the hole: here the cart count arrives within half a second, and everything else is in the shell. The part on partial prerendering times it.

steps.title: Static pages and generateStaticParams
steps.body:
A page that's the same for every visitor should be made once, not once per visitor. Static pages are the fastest and cheapest thing you can serve: no code runs, a CDN can hand them out, and they never fail because a database is slow. So static is where every page should start, and you should only move off it for a reason.

## SSG in Next.js

There's nothing to switch on. A page whose components finish during the build, because they use no request data and their data is cached or fixed, comes out `○`. The about page, which reads a file in the project, and a home page whose data is cached are both static. Recall SSG from the React course: built ahead of time, served as files. That's what `○` is, and with a lifetime in the Revalidate column, it's ISR.

## generateStaticParams

A dynamic route, like `app/products/[slug]`, has one page per value, and the build only renders the values you name. `generateStaticParams`, exported from the page, returns them, and the caching lesson used it to list every product. Each listed slug gets its own prerendered page, with its own entry in the table.

With Cache Components, it must return at least one value, since Next.js renders the route with a real value to check that its shell works. An empty list is a build error. For a big catalog, you don't have to list everything: list the most popular pages, and let the rest be made on first visit.

## Values that weren't listed

A slug that isn't in the list still works. Its first visitor gets the route's App Shell, with the product's parts streaming in, and Next.js keeps the finished page for the next visitor, as the caching lesson showed. If the slug turns out not to exist, the page calls `notFound()`. That first response has already sent its `200`, so it carries the `noindex` tag. Next.js keeps the not-found result too, so the next visit to the same address gets a real `404`. The example below shows both.

Without Cache Components, a setting named `dynamicParams` could refuse unlisted values outright with a `404`. It isn't available with Cache Components: export it, and the build fails, saying the route segment config `dynamicParams` is not compatible with `nextConfig.cacheComponents`. Call `notFound()` for unknown values instead. When even the first response must be a `404`, check the slug in proxy, before rendering starts, as the lesson on Route Handlers and proxy shows.

## When static stops being right

Static pages have two weaknesses, and both come from being made ahead of time:

- **They can be out of date.** A static page shows what was true when it was made. That's fine for an about page, acceptable for a product's description, and wrong for stock or a cart. Data that must be fresh to the second doesn't belong in the shell.
- **They can't know the visitor.** Anything personal, like a name, a cart, or prices in someone's currency from their cookie, can't be in HTML that everyone gets.

When a part of a page has either problem, don't make the whole page dynamic. Make that part a hole, and keep the rest static. That's the next two parts.

examples.title: Listing the product pages
examples.prompt: `app/products/[slug]/page.tsx` lists every product's slug for the build. `listProducts` is cached, so this costs one API call per build.
examples.explanation: Each object is one page's `params`, so `{ slug: "ember-stove" }` becomes `/products/ember-stove`. The build rendered twelve product pages, and the route table listed two and counted the rest. Since the function runs during the build, a product added to the API later isn't listed, but it still works through the App Shell, and the next build will list it. For a route with several dynamic segments, like `[category]/[slug]`, each object holds both.

examples.title: An unlisted slug that doesn't exist
examples.prompt: With the production server running, ask twice for a product nobody sells, and pick out the status line and the robots tag.
examples.code: for i in 1 2; do curl -si http://127.0.0.1:3005/products/tent-9000 | grep -o -E 'HTTP/1.1 [0-9]+ [A-Za-z ]+|<meta name="robots"[^>]*>'; done
examples.explanation: The loop runs the same request twice. The first answer is `200 OK` with `noindex`: the slug wasn't listed, so the shell streamed out with a `200` before the page found out the product doesn't exist. The second answer is `404 Not Found`. After the first render, Next.js stored the result for that address, not-found page and all, and now serves it with the right status straight away. The `noindex` tag stays in it. Search engines see `noindex` either way, so the page never shows up in results.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
<meta name="robots" content="noindex"/>
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
<meta name="robots" content="noindex"/>

steps.title: Dynamic pages
steps.body:
Some pages really are different for every request: an account page, an order history, a search with a hundred thousand possible queries. Rendering them on each request is the only honest option. What matters is how much of the page has to wait for that rendering.

## What makes a route dynamic

Any part of a page that reads request data, `cookies()`, `headers()`, or `searchParams`, renders at request time. So does uncached data from an API or a database, `connection()`, and `params` values that weren't listed. In Next.js 16, that part is a hole in an otherwise prerendered page, so the route is `◐`. Only when a route opts out of the shell altogether, with `export const instant = false`, is it fully dynamic, `ƒ`, the classic server-side rendering from the React course, where the server builds the whole page and sends it.

## Personalized pages

A personalized page is the obvious case: the account page needs the session before it can say who you are. But even there, most of the page isn't personal. The heading, the menu, the layout, the links to orders and settings are the same for everyone. Only the greeting and the order list depend on the cookie. Making those parts holes means the visitor sees the page's frame at once, and their own data a moment later.

## TTFB and cost

Recall TTFB, the time to first byte, from the web course's Network panel. A fully dynamic page's TTFB includes all of its data: the server can't send the heading until it has rendered the page, and it can't render the page until the API answers. Every slow request in it is time the visitor stares at a blank tab. A page with a shell sends the shell immediately, and the slow parts stream after.

There's a cost on the server too. A dynamic page runs your components for every visitor, and calls your API for every visitor, so traffic goes straight through to your backend. A static shell is rendered once, and served from memory or a CDN. On a busy shop, that's the difference between one API call per build and one per visit.

## When to block anyway

Use `instant = false` when a page must not show anything until a check has passed, or when its shell would be empty anyway. Even then, the layout above the page can still have its own holes. For everything else, a hole is the better tool. The examples below are the same account page both ways, timed by when each part of the HTML arrived.

examples.title: An account page that blocks
examples.prompt: `app/account/page.tsx` awaiting the session at the top, with `export const instant = false`. It's `ƒ` in the build. `arrive.mjs` is a small script like the one in the lesson on fetching data, which prints when each phrase first appears in the response. `cookie` holds Sam's session from the login line in that lesson.
examples.explanation: Run it with `node arrive.mjs http://127.0.0.1:3005/account "$cookie" "Trailhead" "Your account" "Signed in as"`, with the Trailhead API started with `TRAILHEAD_DELAYS=1`. All three phrases arrived together, at 201 milliseconds: the site's own header, the page's heading, and the greeting. The server had to wait about 150 milliseconds for the API's `/me` before it could send any of the page's body, so even the parts that are the same for everyone waited. On a slower API, or with more requests in the page, that wait grows, and the tab stays blank the whole time.
examples.output: 201 ms Trailhead 201 ms Your account 201 ms Signed in as

examples.title: The same page with a hole
examples.prompt: The account page from the data lesson, with the greeting inside `Suspense` and no `instant` export. It's `◐` in the build. The same command, run again.
examples.code: node arrive.mjs http://127.0.0.1:3005/account "$cookie" "Trailhead" "Your account" "Signed in as"
examples.explanation: The header and the heading arrived at 23 milliseconds, from the static shell, and the greeting at 176, when the API answered. The total time barely changed, since the data takes as long as it takes. What changed is that the visitor sees the page at once, with Checking who you are… in place of the greeting, instead of a blank tab for most of a fifth of a second. And the server only renders the greeting per request, not the whole page.
examples.output: 23 ms Trailhead 23 ms Your account 176 ms Signed in as

steps.title: Partial prerendering
steps.body:
All-static pages can't show live or personal data, and all-dynamic pages make everyone wait for the slowest part. Partial prerendering takes the best of both inside one page, and with Cache Components it's how Next.js builds every route by default. The product page is where it pays off most.

## A shell with holes

A partially prerendered page has two kinds of content. The **static shell** is everything that's the same for every visitor, rendered during the build or regenerated later, and sent as soon as a request arrives. The **holes** are the parts that need the request, rendered on each one and streamed into the same response as they finish. The visitor never sees a blank page: the shell is there in milliseconds, with fallbacks in the holes, and the holes fill in a moment later.

```diagram rendering-modes-ppr
The shell holds everything shared. Two holes, the stock and the cart count, fill in per request.
```

Trailhead's product page has two holes. The stock line, with the quantity picker, reads `getStock`, which is uncached so it's never out of date. The cart count in the header reads the visitor's cookie. Everything else is in the shell: the header's links, the product's name and price from the cached `getProduct`, and the reviews from the cached `getReviews`.

## The holes are Suspense boundaries

There's no new API to learn. A hole is a `Suspense` boundary with something inside that waits for the request, and its fallback is what the shell shows in its place. Where you put the boundaries decides the page's shape: everything outside every boundary must finish during the build, and each boundary marks where a hole begins. That's why the build error from the caching lesson offers `[stream]` as a fix: wrapping a part in `Suspense` turns it into a hole.

Make holes small, and give their fallbacks the same size as their content, so nothing jumps when they fill in. A hole that wraps half the page gives you half a shell.

## Why it beats all or nothing

Compare the product page three ways. All static, the stock would be as old as the last build, and the cart count would have to be fetched in the browser after hydration. All dynamic, every visitor would wait for the product, the reviews, the stock, and the cart before seeing anything, and every visit would call the API four times. Partial, the visitor sees the product at once from the shell, the API is called twice per visit for the two things that must be fresh, and the page is never stale where it matters.

## Where it runs

On your own server, `next start` keeps the shell in memory and sends it at once, then renders the holes. Some hosting platforms can serve the shell from their CDN and stream the holes from your server, which brings the first bytes even closer to the visitor. Either way, the response's `Cache-Control` says `private`, since the finished page holds personal parts, and that's correct: the shell is cached by Next.js, not by a shared cache that doesn't know about holes. The deployment lesson covers what each kind of host supports.

examples.title: The product page's stock hole
examples.prompt: Part of `app/products/[slug]/page.tsx`. The product and the reviews come from cached functions. The stock is read fresh, inside its own boundary.
examples.explanation: The comment shows where `Stock` sits in the page: inside `Suspense`, with a fallback the same height as the stock line. `getStock` isn't cached, so this component is the hole, and the build renders the fallback into the shell instead. The quantity picker moved in here from the page, since its maximum depends on the stock. The header's cart count works the same way: `<Suspense fallback={<Link href="/cart">Cart</Link>}>` around a `CartCount` Server Component that reads the cart with `apiFetch("/cart", { session: true })`. In the Server Components lesson the badge counted items in a browser store, and now it shows the API's count for the logged-in visitor.

examples.title: Timing the shell and the holes
examples.prompt: `holes.mjs` is like the script from the lesson on fetching data, but sends a session cookie and prints only chunks that hold one of six phrases. Sam's cart holds one Ember Stove and two Trail Runner Caps, put there with the API's `PUT /v1/cart/items/{slug}`. Run it against the product page as Sam.
examples.explanation: At 26 milliseconds the shell has arrived, with the name, the reviews, the Checking stock… fallback, and the header's plain Cart link, which the script finds as `>Cart<`. Those are all from the prerendered shell, so no API call was needed for them. At 228 the stock hole fills with In stock. At 427 the cart hole fills with Cart (3), after the API's cart answered. The last line is the RSC payload for hydration, which repeats the shell's text. In the lesson on fetching data the reviews took 927 milliseconds. Now they're in the shell, since they're cached, and the slowest thing left is the cart.

26 ms  Ember Stove, Checking stock…, Boils fast, >Cart<
   26 ms  Ember Stove, Checking stock…, Boils fast
  228 ms  In stock
  228 ms  In stock
  427 ms  Cart (3)
  427 ms  Cart (3)

steps.title: Client rendering and static export
steps.body:
Some parts of a page only make sense in the browser, and some sites don't need a server at all. Next.js handles both, and knowing the limits keeps you from reaching for them when a hole would do.

## Client rendering, where it fits

Client-side rendering is still the right tool for parts that depend on the browser itself: something saved in `localStorage`, the window's size, a map or a chart library that only runs with a DOM, or live updates over a socket. In Next.js, those are client components that fetch or read after hydration, in effects or with TanStack Query, as the data lesson's last part described. They render a fallback on the server and fill in once they're in the browser.

## next/dynamic with ssr: false

A client component still renders on the server first, which breaks for code that touches `window` or `localStorage` while rendering. `dynamic` from `next/dynamic` loads a component lazily, and with `ssr: false` it skips the server render entirely: the server sends the `loading` placeholder, and the browser downloads the component's code and renders it after hydration. In the App Router, `ssr: false` only works inside a client component, so the `dynamic()` call lives in a small client file. The component's code also moves into its own chunk, so it costs nothing on pages that don't show it.

## Static export

`output: "export"` in `next.config.ts` turns `next build` into a generator of plain files, written to the `out` folder: HTML for each page, plus the JavaScript and CSS. Any static file host can serve them, with no Node.js server at all. It's a fine fit for a documentation site or a marketing site.

The price is everything that needs a server at request time. No cookies or headers, no holes that render per request, no Route Handlers beyond GET handlers that can run at build time, no Server Actions, no proxy, no ISR, and no image optimization on the fly. Pages with unlisted dynamic values can't work either, since there's no server to render them. Trailhead can't be exported: the build stops at the first page that reads a cookie, as the example shows. A site that needs any of those needs `next start` or a platform that runs Next.js.

## Choosing a mode for each page

| Page | Mode | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| About, help, policies | Static, `○` | The same for everyone, changes with a deploy |
| Home, product list | Static with a lifetime (ISR) | Shared, changes a few times a day |
| Product page | Partial, `◐` | Shared details in the shell, stock and cart as holes |
| Search results | Partial, `◐` | The shell is shared, results depend on the query |
| Account, orders | Partial, `◐`, or dynamic, `ƒ` | Personal, but the frame can still be a shell |
| Recently viewed | Client, with `ssr: false` | Lives in the browser's storage |
| A docs site with no server | Static export | Plain files on any host |

Start each page static, add holes for what must be fresh or personal, and reach for `ƒ` or the client only when a hole can't do the job. Then check the route table to see that you got what you meant.

examples.title: A component that only renders in the browser
examples.prompt: `components/recently-viewed-loader.tsx` loads `components/recently-viewed.tsx`, which reads `localStorage` while it renders, without a server render. The about page renders `<RecentlyViewedLoader />`.
examples.explanation: `recently-viewed.tsx` is a client component whose default export reads a list of slugs from `localStorage` and shows them. On the server, `localStorage` doesn't exist, so rendering it there would crash. With `ssr: false`, the server's HTML has only the empty `loading` paragraph, which holds the line's space, and a search of the about page's HTML found no Recently viewed text. In the browser, after hydration, the component's chunk loads and renders: with two slugs saved, the page showed Recently viewed: ember-stove, ridge-2p-tent. The about page itself stayed in the static shell.

examples.title: Trying to export Trailhead
examples.prompt: With `output: "export"` added to `next.config.ts`, run the build. The output below starts where the error does.
examples.explanation: The export stops at the first page it renders that reads request data, here `/catalog`, whose header has the cart count that reads the session cookie. An export forces `dynamic = "error"` on every page, a setting from before Cache Components that means fail rather than render per request, and the message names it. Every page has that header, so fixing `/catalog` wouldn't help: the cart count would have to move to the browser, along with the stock, the account page, and the revalidation webhook. That's the sign a site isn't a static site. Take `output: "export"` back out, and it builds again. Every page so far only reads. The next section turns to writes, starting with the forms that change data through Server Actions.
examples.output:
Error occurred prerendering page "/catalog". Read more: https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/prerender-error
Error: Route /catalog with `dynamic = "error"` couldn't be rendered statically because it used `cookies()`. See more info here: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/rendering/static-and-dynamic#dynamic-rendering
Export encountered an error on /catalog/page: /catalog, exiting the build.
⨯ Next.js build worker exited with code: 1 and signal: null

recap:
- The route table shows ○ for static, ◐ for a shell with holes, and ƒ for fully dynamic, with each page's shortest Revalidate and Expire.
- One hole in a shared layout makes every page under it ◐, while the rest stays prerendered.
- Static pages need nothing switched on, and generateStaticParams lists a dynamic route's values for the build.
- dynamicParams isn't available with Cache Components. Call notFound() for unknown values, or check them in proxy.
- A fully dynamic page waits for all its data before the first byte of its body, so prefer holes.
- Partial prerendering sends the shell at once and streams each Suspense boundary's content per request.
- next/dynamic with ssr: false renders browser-only components after hydration, and output: "export" works only without request-time features.
- Start every page static, add holes for fresh or personal parts, and check the route table.
